sudan.content: من بشريات أكتوبر 2020 إلى السقوط الحر في أكتوبر 2026 - سودان تربيون تخطى الى المحتوى من نحن اتصل بنا English الأربعاء , 21 أكتوبر - 2026 سودان تربيون أخبار السودان وتقارير حصرية لحظة بلحظة الرئيسية سياسة الأخبار تقصي الحقائق اقتصاد دولي اقاليم الرأي English سودان تربيون أخبار السودان وتقارير حصرية لحظة بلحظة الرئيسية الرأي من بشريات أكتوبر 2020 إلى السقوط الحر في أكتوبر 2026 الرأي من بشريات أكتوبر 2020 إلى السقوط الحر في أكتوبر 2026 21 أكتوبر 2026 في الرأي 0 صورة تعبيرية د. سليمان علي أين كنا وأين وصلنا؟ ستة أعوام بين الأمل الذي كان يطرق أبواب السودان، وبين الواقع الذي يطرق أبواب السودانيين بالفقر والعجز وفقدان اليقين الوطني. في العشرين من أكتوبر 2020، كتبنا ونحن نستقبل ذكرى الحادي والعشرين من أكتوبر، وكنا نرى في الأفق ملامح وطن يلتقط أنفاسه بعد عقود من الاختناق والحصار والعقوبات الدولية. ↔️ كان الانتقال منصة جديدة للبناء القومي:_ كان السودان يومها يخطو خطواته الأولى في مرحلة انتقالية مثقلة بالتحديات، لكنه كان يمتلك شيئًا جوهريًا: الأمل في أن تكون الثورة بداية لتأسيس دولة جديدة، وأن تتحول تضحيات الشهداء إلى واقع يلمسه الناس في معاشهم وحريتهم وكرامتهم. كانت كلمات ذلك اليوم تحمل شيئًا من نشوة الانتصار؛ «يا أكتوبر الأرض تغني وباسمك الشعب انتصر، وحائط السجن انكسر». وكانت إزالة اسم السودان من قائمة الدول الراعية للإرهاب إحدى العلامات البارزة التي استقبل بها السودانيون تلك المرحلة، باعتبارها نافذة للخروج من العزلة الدولية، واستعادة العلاقات الاقتصادية والمالية، وفتح الطريق أمام فرص جديدة للتعافي وإعادة بناء الدولة. لم يكن السودان في عام 2020 دولة مكتملة العافية، ولم تكن أحوال الناس الاقتصادية مثالية، بل كانت الأزمات المعيشية والتضخم واختلالات الاقتصاد حاضرة بقوة. لكن الفارق أن البلاد كانت لديها فرصة سياسية للانتقال، وتوقعات بإصلاح المؤسسات، واستعادة الإنتاج، وبناء اقتصاد يخدم المواطنين بدلًا من أن يكون عبئًا إضافيًا على حياتهم. أما اليوم، في أكتوبر 2026، فالسؤال الذي يفرض نفسه كيف وصلنا إلى هنا؟ ستة أعوام كانت كافية لتكشف المسافة الهائلة بين الوعود التي حملتها المرحلة الانتقالية، والواقع الذي انتهى إليه السودان. تدهورت الحالة الوطنية إلى مستوى سحيق، وتآكلت القدرة الشرائية للعملة إلى حد باتت معه الدخول التي كانت توفر الحد الأدنى من متطلبات الحياة عاجزة عن ملاحقة الأسعار. فقد الناس قيمة جهدهم وعرقهم، وأصبحت المرتبات أرقامًا على الورق، لا تعكس قدرة حقيقية على توفير الغذاء والدواء والسكن والتعليم. لم تعد الأزمة مجرد ارتفاع في الأسعار، ولا مجرد انخفاض في سعر العملة. إنها أزمة اقتصاد فقد قدرته على حماية قيمة العمل، وأزمة دولة تراجعت قدرتها على تنظيم النشاط الاقتصادي وتوفير الخدمات وضمان الحد الأدنى من الاستقرار. حين يعمل الإنسان شهرًا كاملًا ثم يكتشف أن ما يتقاضاه لا يكفي احتياجات أسرته الأساسية، فإن الخلل يتجاوز ميزانية الأسرة إلى بنية الاقتصاد والسياسات التي تحكمه. وفي الوقت الذي كان يفترض أن تتجه فيه البلاد إلى توسيع الإنتاج الزراعي والصناعي، وتطوير البنية التحتية، وتهيئة بيئة الاستثمار، اتسعت دائرة الفشل والانكماش الاقتصادي، وتراجعت قدرات قطاعات واسعة على العمل والإنتاج. وأصبح نشاط المضاربات في الأراضي والعملات، في ظل اختلالات السوق وانعدام الاستقرار، ملاذًا لبعض رؤوس الأموال، بينما تحمل المنتجون والمزارعون والعمال وأصحاب الأعمال الصغيرة كلفة الانهيار. ↔️ الحرب وعوامل سابقة لها تتحمل ما يجري الان؟ لقد انتقل السودان من سؤال كيفية استثمار الفرصة التي أتاحها الانفتاح الدولي؟ ، إلى سؤال كيفية حماية ما تبقى من مقومات الحياة؟. وبين السؤالين ضاعت سنوات ثمينة، وتراكمت الأزمات، وانفتح الباب أمام حرب مدمرة لم تكتفِ بإيقاف مسار الانتقال، بل ألحقت أضرارًا واسعة بالمؤسسات والأسواق وسبل العيش، ودفعت ملايين السودانيين إلى النزوح واللجوء وفقدان مصادر دخلهم. ومع ذلك، فإن اختزال كل ما حدث في الحرب وحدها لا يقدم تفسيرًا كاملًا للمأساة. فالحرب كانت عاملًا مدمرًا ومسرّعًا للانهيار، لكنها جاءت فوق أرضية من هشاشة المؤسسات، وأزمة الحكم، وضعف بناء التوافق الوطني، وتعثر الإصلاح الاقتصادي، وعجز القوى السياسية عن تحويل شعارات الثورة إلى مشروع دولة تتجاوز صراعات السلطة ومصالح الجماعات. هنا تكمن المأساة الحقيقية: لم تكن المشكلة في غياب الموارد، فالسودان بلد واسع الإمكانات الزراعية والحيوانية والمعدنية، ويمتلك موقعًا جغرافيًا استراتيجيًا وموارد بشرية قادرة على الإسهام في نهضته. وإنما كانت المشكلة، ولا تزال، في كيفية إدارة هذه الموارد، وفي طبيعة السلطة التي تتحكم فيها، وفي غياب مشروع وطني يجعل الإنتاج أولوية، ويضع مصالح المواطنين فوق حسابات التمكين والاحتكار والصراع. أين كنا وأين وصلنا؟ كان السودان في أكتوبر 2020 يتطلع إلى كسر العزلة، واستعادة موقعه في المجتمع الدولي، وفتح الطريق أمام التعافي الاقتصادي. أما في أكتوبر 2026، فإن السودانيين يواجهون تحديات البقاء، ويبحثون عن الأمن والغذاء والدواء ومصادر الرزق، بينما يحتاج الوطن إلى إعادة بناء ما دمرته الحرب، وإصلاح ما أفسدته سنوات الاختلال السياسي والاقتصادي. كان الأمل أن تنكسر جدران العزلة، وأن تتسع أمام البلاد أبواب المستقبل. لكن ما حدث أن جدرانًا أخرى ارتفعت: جدران الحرب، والانقسام، والفقر، وانعدام الثقة، وتراجع القدرة على الحلم. ولعل أكثر ما يستحق المراجعة اليوم هو أن إزالة اسم السودان من قائمة الدول الراعية للإرهاب لم تكن، في حد ذاتها، مشروعًا للنهضة، بل كانت فرصة تحتاج إلى رؤية اقتصادية، واستقرار سياسي، ومؤسسات قادرة على تحويل الانفتاح الدولي إلى إنتاج وفرص عمل وتحسن في مستوى المعيشة. فالانفتاح لا يبني دولة بمفرده، ورفع القيود لا يعوض غياب السياسات، كما أن الشعارات الثورية لا تغني عن بناء المؤسسات. ↔️ كيف نضع الوطن في منصة انطلاق جديدة؟ إن استعادة الوطن، تحتاج إلى مشروع وطني طموح يعيد تعريف أولويات الدولة: حماية الإنسان، واستعادة المؤسسات، وإحياء الإنتاج، وإصلاح النظام المالي، وإعادة بناء الخدمات، وتوزيع السلطة والثروة بعدالة، وتأسيس حكم يستمد شرعيته من المواطنين وقدرته على خدمتهم. وتحتاج هذه المهمة إلى مراجعة شجاعة لتجربة السنوات الماضية، لا بهدف تبادل الاتهامات أو تصفية الحسابات، وإنما لتحديد المسؤوليات ولفهم كيف تحولت فرصة تاريخية إلى مأساة وطنية، ولماذا عجزت القوى التي رفعت شعارات التغيير عن حماية المسار الذي بشرت به، وكيف تقدمت حسابات السلطة على مطلوبات حماية الثورة والانتقال الديمقراطي وبناء دولة كل السودانيين. أكتوبر ليس مجرد ذكرى في التقويم السياسي السوداني، ولا أغنية تستعاد كل عام، بل هو سؤال متجدد عن معنى الثورة، وعن العلاقة بين تضحيات الشعب والنتائج التي يجنيها. وإذا كانت أكتوبر 1964 قد حملت وعدًا بالخلاص من الاستبداد، وكانت ديسمبر 2018 تعبيرًا عن تطلع جيل جديد إلى الحرية والسلام والعدالة، فإن مسؤوليتنا اليوم أن نمنع تحول هذه التضحيات إلى مجرد صفحات في تاريخ وطن أضاع فرصه. أين كانت البلد وأين وصلت؟ كان الحلم أن ينتقل السودان من العزلة إلى الانفتاح، ومن الاستبداد إلى الحكم المدني، ومن اقتصاد الأزمات إلى اقتصاد الإنتاج. واليوم، بعد ستة أعوام، نقف أمام سؤال أشد إيلامًا: كيف نحول ما تبقى من الوطن إلى بداية جديدة؟ ، بدلًا من أن نترك الانهيار يكتب خاتمة الحلم؟ إن السودان لا يحتاج إلى استعادة صور أكتوبر 2020 وحدها، بل إلى استعادة المعنى الذي جعل السودانيين يؤمنون بأن التغيير ممكن. يحتاج إلى دولة لا تهدر قيمة العمل، ولا تبدد الموارد، ولا تجعل المواطن يدفع ثمن فشل النخب وصراعاتها. يحتاج إلى مشروع وطني يتجاوز الحرب، ويؤسس لسلام مستدام، واقتصاد منتج، وعدالة في توزيع السلطة والثروة، ومؤسسات تحمي الجميع دون استثناء. فالمجد للشهداء لا يكون بترديد أسمائهم فحسب، وإنما ببناء الوطن الذي استشهدوا من أجله. والتقدم لا يقاس بما نعلنه من انتصارات، بل بما يستعيده المواطن من أمن وكرامة وقدرة على العيش. أكتوبر الذي غنّى له السودان بالأمس، يجب أن يكون اليوم مناسبة لمراجعة المسار، ومواجهة الحقيقة، واستعادة الوطن من قبضة الحرب والفشل والانقسام. فالسؤال الجوهري اليوم: هل نملك الإرادة لبناء سودان جديد؟ ، أم سنظل نستهلك ذكريات الانتصارات بينما تتآكل مقومات الحياة أمام أعيننا؟ مقالات ذات صلة مغالطات sudan.summary: تتناول المقالة الفجوة الكبيرة بين الأمل الذي ساد في أكتوبر 2020 والواقع المرير الذي يعيشه السودانيون في أكتوبر 2026. في عام 2020، كان هناك تفاؤل بإمكانية بناء دولة جديدة بعد إزالة اسم السودان من قائمة الدول الراعية للإرهاب، مما فتح آفاقًا للتعافي الاقتصادي. ومع ذلك، بعد ست سنوات، تدهورت الأوضاع بشكل كبير، حيث ارتفعت معدلات الفقر والعجز، وفقدت العملة قيمتها، مما جعل الرواتب غير كافية لتلبية احتياجات الحياة الأساسية. كما تفاقمت الأزمات الاقتصادية والسياسية، مما أدى إلى نزوح الملايين واندلاع حرب مدمرة. تشدد المقالة على ضرورة إعادة بناء الدولة من خلال مشروع وطني يركز على حماية المواطنين واستعادة المؤسسات، بدلاً من الاكتفاء بالذكريات والانتصارات السابقة.

sudan.content: سياسي / نائب وزير الخارجية يشارك في الاجتماع التشاوري السادس بشأن تعزيز تنسيق مبادرات وجهود السلام في السودان
sudan.summary: شارك نائب وزير الخارجية في الاجتماع التشاوري السادس الذي يهدف إلى تعزيز تنسيق المبادرات والجهود الرامية إلى تحقيق السلام في السودان. يأتي هذا الاجتماع في إطار الجهود الدولية والمحلية لدعم الاستقرار في البلاد، حيث تم مناقشة التحديات الحالية وسبل تعزيز التعاون بين الأطراف المعنية. يهدف الاجتماع إلى توحيد الجهود وتعزيز التنسيق بين مختلف المبادرات لتحقيق نتائج إيجابية في عملية السلام.

اليوم الأربعاء إلى أدنى مستوى ⁠لها عند 10 آلاف جنيه مقابل الدولار في السوق الموازية، وفق رويترز، لتواصل الهبوط الحاد الذي حققته في الشهور القليلة ⁠الماضية في ظل تأثر الاقتصاد بضغوط الحرب. وأدى الانخفاض المتواصل في سعر صرف الجنيه السوداني مقابل الدولار إلى تفاقم معاناة السودانيين، مع الارتفاع في الأسعار، ⁠في وقت يحاولون فيه التكيف مع الظروف القاسية التي فرضتها الحرب بين القوات المسلحة السودانية وقوات الدعم السريع، التي تسببت في نزوح الملايين من مساكنهم، وجعلت المواد الغذائية الأساسية بعيدة عن متناول ‌أيديهم. قصص مقترحة list of 4 items list 1 of 4 تفكيك أسباب أزمة الجوع في السودان العائدون إلى الخرطوم؟ end of list ولا يزال سعر الصرف الرسمي في السودان عند 4200 جنيه للدولار، وهو مستوى شوهد آخر مرة في السوق الموازية في المناطق الخاضعة لسيطرة الجيش في مايو/أيار الماضي، حسب ما ذكرته اندلاع الحرب في أبريل/نيسان 2023. الحرب تسببت في نزوح ملايين السودانيين مما أدى لتراجع الإنتاج بمخلف القطاعات (غيتي) تراجع الإنتاج وزيادة الواردات وأشار تجار عملة إلى أن الطلب على الاستيراد هو ⁠العامل الرئيسي وراء التراجع السريع في سعر صرف الجنيه السوداني مقابل الدولار. ورفعت الحكومة سعر الدولار الجمركي، الخاضع لرقابة صارمة والمستخدم ⁠لحساب الرسوم الجمركية على سلع أساسية، إلى أكثر من ⁠5600 جنيه للدولار الواحد هذا الأسبوع. ومع استمرار الحرب، خفض السودان إنتاج قطاعات تعد من المصادر الرئيسية للدولار، في حين يتزايد تهريب الذهب إلى الخارج، وهو ‌أهم سلعة تصدرها البلاد. وفي الوقت نفسه، قالت الحكومة السودانية إن الحرب وجهود إعادة الإعمار تتطلب ‌واردات ‌تستنزف الدولار، علاوة على الواردات من السلع الغذائية التي تراجع إنتاجها بسبب الحرب. إعلان كما تسببت الحرب في السودان في انقسام واضح في المشهد الاقتصادي والمالي، مع تفاوت طرق التداول والسيولة النقدية بين مناطق سيطرة الجيش السودان و قوات الدعم السريع . وأوضح تقرير سابق للجزيرة نت أن التداول التجاري في مناطق خاضعة لسيطرة الدعم السريع، ولا سيما البرهان الخرطوم 21 أكتوبر 2026 – أصدر رئيس مجلس السيادة الانتقالي، الفريق أول ركن عبد الفتاح البرهان، قراراً بإعادة المؤسسة السودانية للنفط، بعد سبع سنوات من حلها. وتضطلع المؤسسة بدور استراتيجي في تنمية الثروة النفطية وحسن استغلالها، من خلال أعمال الاستكشاف والإنتاج، فضلاً عن توفير احتياجات البلاد من المواد البترولية المختلفة وتأمين المخزون الاستراتيجي. وَقال بيان صحفي لوزارة الطاقة والنفط الأربعاء إن رئيس مجلس السيادة عبد الفتاح البرهان أصدر قراراً بإعادة “المؤسسة السودانية للنفط”، بعد سبع سنوات من حلها في العام 2019. وجاء القرار في إطار جهود الدولة لإصلاح وإعادة تنظيم قطاع الطاقة وتفعيل قانون الثروة النفطية وإعادة تكوين مجلس النفط برئاسة رئيس مجلس السيادة، ويضم في عضويته قيادات عليا وجهات اختصاص سيادية واقتصادية وأمنية. ويضم مجلس النفط وزراء النفط والمالية والعدل، ومدير جهاز المخابرات العامة، ورئيس جهاز الاستثمار الوطني، إلى جانب عدد محدود من خبراء النفط، بما يجمع الجهات السيادية والاقتصادية والفنية ذات الصلة بالقطاع. وفي السياق ذاته، أصدر البرهان قراراً بتعيين اللواء بحري المتقاعد الدكتور إسماعيل عثمان الحسين أبوشوك أميناً عاماً للمؤسسة السودانية للنفط. وكان بنك السودان المركزي وافق، في ديسمبر 2025، على تعيين أبوشوك مديراً عاماً لبنك النيلين المملوك للدولة، غير أن القرار أثار جدلاً في الأوساط الاقتصادية والمصرفية بشأن مدى صلته بالقطاع المصرفي، الذي يتطلب تولي قياداته خبرات متخصصة. واعتذر أبوشوك لاحقاً عن تولي المنصب، عقب انتقادات لتعيين عسكريين متقاعدين في إدارة البنوك والمصارف. وتدرج أبوشوك في الرتب العسكرية منذ تخرجه في الدفعة 29، حتى وصل إلى رتبة لواء قبل إحالته إلى التقاعد، كما حصل أثناء الخدمة على درجة الدكتوراه في مجال العلوم العسكرية البحرية. وفي سبتمبر 2023، تقدم أبوشوك، ضمن مجموعة من الضباط المتقاعدين، بمذكرة إلى رئيس مجلس السيادة والقائد العام للقوات المسلحة، عبد الفتاح البرهان، أعلنوا فيها تأييدهم لتفويضه بالقضاء على قوات الدعم السريع والاستمرار في الدفاع عن حقوق المواطنين. وأُنشئت المؤسسة السودانية للنفط بموجب قانون الثروة النفطية لعام 1998، بوصفها مؤسسة عامة تتمتع بشخصية اعتبارية مستقلة، ويقع مقرها في الخرطوم. وكانت تخضع لسلطات مجلس النفط، الذي كان يرأسه رئيس الجمهورية، تحت إشراف وزير النفط، قبل أن تُحل في عام 2019. مقالات ذات صلة البرهان يجدد تحذيراته ويؤكد التزام (الحرية والتغيير) بالابتعاد عن السلطة لجنة التحقيق في دعم بالهجرة إلى أوروبا عبر قوراب غير آمنة بروكسل 21 أكتوبر 2026 – كشفت وكالة الاتحاد الأوروبي للجوء، الأربعاء، عن تقديم نحو 31 ألف سوداني طلبات لجوء في دول الاتحاد الأوروبي خلال 17 شهرًا، منها 11 ألف طلب لا يزال قيد انتظار البت فيها. ويدفع استمرار النزاع آلاف السودانيين إلى سلوك مسارات هجرة عالية الخطورة عبر البحر الأبيض المتوسط، بغرض الوصول إلى أوروبا، في ظل ضعف تلبية احتياجاتهم في دول الجوار ومخاطر الحماية داخل السودان. وقالت الوكالة، في تقرير، إن “المواطنين السودانيين تقدموا خلال الفترة من مارس 2025 إلى أغسطس 2026 بنحو 31 ألف طلب لجوء في بلدان الاتحاد الأوروبي والدول المرتبطة به ضمن منظومة الاتحاد الأوروبي للجوء”. وأوضح التقرير أن اليونان وفرنسا استقبلتا أكثر من ثلاثة أرباع الطلبات المقدمة، بواقع 13 ألف طلب في اليونان و11 ألف طلب في فرنسا. وأشار إلى أن دول الاتحاد الأوروبي والدول المرتبطة به أصدرت نحو 20 ألف قرار ابتدائي بشأن طلبات لجوء تقدم بها مواطنون سودانيون، حيث تصدرت اليونان وفرنسا قائمة الدول من حيث عدد القرارات، بواقع 8 آلاف قرار في اليونان و7900 قرار في فرنسا. وأفاد التقرير بأنه حتى مطلع أغسطس 2026، كان أكثر من 11 ألف طلب لجوء لمواطنين سودانيين لا يزال قيد الانتظار لاتخاذ قرار بشأنه في المرحلة الابتدائية، من بينها نحو 5400 طلب في اليونان. وتدفع الحرب آلاف السودانيين إلى سلوك مسارات الهجرة عبر البحر الأبيض المتوسط انطلاقًا من ليبيا ومصر، وسط تزايد الاعتماد على اليونان نقطةَ دخول رئيسية إلى أوروبا. وذكرت الوكالة أن طلبات اللجوء المقدمة من السودانيين بدأت في الارتفاع مع اندلاع الحرب في أبريل 2023، قبل أن تسجل زيادة حادة خلال عام 2025. وبينت أن طلبات لجوء السودانيين واصلت اتجاهها التصاعدي خلال الأشهر الثمانية الأولى من عام 2026، إذ بلغ عددها نحو 15 ألف طلب، بزيادة تقارب الثلثين مقارنة بالفترة نفسها من عام 2025. وفي 19 سبتمبر الماضي، قالت مفوضية الأمم المتحدة لشؤون اللاجئين إن سودانيين تعرضوا لانتهاكات خلال رحلات لجوئهم إلى أوروبا، شملت الاحتجاز والتعذيب والاستغلال والاتجار بالبشر. تعثر الوساطة والانتهاكات ونشرت وكالة الاتحاد الأوروبي للجوء، في أكتوبر 2026، تقريرًا تناول الأوضاع الأمنية واتجاهات الصراع والجهات الفاعلة الرئيسية على المستويين الوطني والإقليمي في السودان. وأفاد التقرير بأن أكثر من 3 سنوات من الحرب بين الجيش وقوات الدعم السريع أدت إلى مزيد من تفتت السلطة في البلاد، في ظل إخفاق جهود الوساطة الدولية في التوصل إلى وقف دائم لإطلاق النار. وأوضح أن جهود الوساطة شملت الاتحاد الأفريقي والهيئة الحكومية الدولية المعنية بالتنمية “إيغاد”، إلى جانب الولايات المتحدة والسعودية ومصر والإمارات وسويسرا. وأرجع التقرير تعثر هذه الجهود إلى الخلافات بين الأطراف الخارجية، ورفض الجيش التفاوض مع قوات الدعم السريع على قدم المساواة، فضلًا عن تضارب المصالح السياسية. وتحدث التقرير عن استمرار تعرض المدنيين لأعمال عنف واسعة النطاق وانتهاكات لحقوق الإنسان، شملت القتل خارج نطاق القضاء والاحتجاز التعسفي والاختفاء القسري والتعذيب والعنف الجنسي. وأفاد بأن نحو 19.5 مليون شخص واجهوا انعدام الأمن الغذائي الحاد خلال عامي 2025 و2026، فيما تأثرت مناطق عدة بالمجاعة أو بخطر حدوثها. كما افتقر 17 مليون شخص إلى مياه الشرب المأمونة، ما زاد من مخاطر تفشي الأمراض وسوء التغذية. وأشار إلى أن الحرب ألحقت أضرارًا بالبنية التحتية الزراعية وعطلت سلاسل الإمداد، بينما أسهم ارتفاع أسعار المواد الغذائية في تفاقم الجوع، فيما واجه إيصال المساعدات الإنسانية قيودًا كبيرة بسبب الهجمات المسلحة والعوائق البيروقراطية وإغلاق الطرق ونقص التمويل. الكلمات: الاتحاد Attending Kenya’s Mashujaa Day celebrations as President William Ruto’s guest of honour, Abiy emphasized the longstanding partnership between the two countries, highlighting cooperation in electricity, telecommunications, trade and regional connectivity. Yet beyond the diplomatic celebrations, the visit coincided with growing tensions involving Somalia, whose internal political crisis has begun complicating its relations with both Ethiopia and Kenya. Although Abiy’s visit was officially centered on Kenya’s Mashujaa Day celebrations and bilateral cooperation, it unfolded against a backdrop of growing regional tensions involving Somalia. The visit did not publicly establish a common Ethiopian and Kenyan position on the Somali crisis, but it brought renewed attention to the strategic importance of their partnership as both countries navigate increasingly complicated relations with Mogadishu. The significance of Ethiopia’s relationship with Kenya extends beyond bilateral cooperation. Both countries have invested considerable military and diplomatic resources in Somalia’s stabilization, particularly in efforts to contain Al Shabaab and prevent insecurity from spreading across their borders. However, Somalia’s confrontation between its federal government and regional political actors is creating disagreements over the responsibilities of neighbouring countries. For Ethiopia, the challenge is to maintain its commitment to Somalia’s security without becoming involved in political disputes that could undermine its wider regional interests. The immediate source of tension lies in Somalia’s South West State, where the removal of former regional president Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed Laftagareen in March 2026 failed to produce a lasting political settlement. Instead, confrontations between his supporters and forces aligned with the federal government have continued, exposing deeper disagreements over regional autonomy and the distribution of political authority. By October 19, forces loyal to Laftagareen reportedly controlled five towns in the Bay region, including Buurhakaba, Qansaxdheere and Dinsoor, complicating Mogadishu’s efforts to consolidate authority. The conflict is particularly consequential because the South West State includes territories where Ethiopian forces have maintained a security presence for years. According to Somali Guardian reporting published on October 19 , Somali federal authorities requested Ethiopian military assistance against forces aligned with Laftagareen, but Ethiopian commanders declined to participate in what they considered an internal political confrontation. Although the reported exchange has not been independently confirmed, it illustrates a fundamental question concerning foreign military involvement in Somalia: whether security assistance intended to confront common threats should extend to supporting the federal government in disputes over domestic political authority. For Ethiopia, the issue has acquired additional importance following the transition from the African Union Transition Mission in Somalia, ATMIS, to the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia, AUSSOM, which commenced on January 1, 2025. Under United Nations Security Council Resolution 2767 , the successor mission was authorized to support Somali forces against Al Shabaab, protect civilians and facilitate the gradual transfer of security responsibilities to Somali institutions. Its mandate also encompasses security support for political processes, but does not provide unrestricted authority to determine the outcome of internal political disputes. The transition brought renewed attention to the distinction between Ethiopian troops operating under African Union arrangements and those deployed through separate bilateral security understandings. This distinction matters because forces assigned to AUSSOM operate within a defined multinational framework, while deployments outside that structure depend on separate arrangements with Somalia. In its December 2025 communiqué , the African Union Peace and Security Council explicitly acknowledged Ethiopia and Uganda for deploying additional troops under bilateral arrangements. Their presence cannot therefore be understood solely through AUSSOM’s command structure. Ethiopia’s longstanding involvement in Somalia has primarily been driven by the need to prevent Al Shabaab from developing secure operating areas near Ethiopian territory. The group’s ability to exploit instability and threaten communities across borders makes developments in Somalia directly relevant to Ethiopia’s national security. Ethiopian military operations and participation in successive African Union missions have consequently contributed to a broader effort to contain threats before they reach Ethiopian territory. The South West State remains especially important because the Bay and Bakool regions form part of the wider security environment connected to Ethiopia’s eastern frontier. Participation in Somalia’s internal political confrontations, however, would expose Ethiopia to different risks. Military intervention could associate Ethiopian forces with one Somali political faction, weaken relationships with local communities and transform a defined security commitment into an extended responsibility for political outcomes. Even a successful intervention would not necessarily resolve disagreements concerning federal authority and regional political representation. Somalia’s domestic disputes require political settlements that military involvement by neighbouring countries cannot independently deliver. This position should not be confused with opposition to Somalia’s federal government. Addis Ababa and Mogadishu continue to maintain diplomatic relations and share an interest in preventing renewed militant expansion. Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s September 29 visit to Addis Ababa , during which he discussed bilateral relations and regional security with Abiy Ahmed, demonstrated the continued importance of diplomatic engagement despite existing disagreements. Those disagreements nevertheless have a deeper history. The January 2024 memorandum of understanding between Ethiopia and Somaliland, which addressed potential Ethiopian maritime access, produced a significant confrontation with Mogadishu over sovereignty and territorial integrity. Somalia regarded the arrangement as an infringement on its sovereignty, while Ethiopia viewed access to the sea as an important strategic and economic objective. The dispute contributed to Somalia’s closer security engagement with Egypt, which already maintained long winded Nile disagreements with Ethiopia. The December 2024 Ankara Declaration , facilitated by Türkiye, helped restore diplomatic engagement by reaffirming mutual respect for sovereignty and acknowledging the possibility of mutually beneficial maritime arrangements under Somalia’s sovereign authority. Nevertheless, restoring diplomatic communication did not eliminate competing regional security calculations. Egypt’s expanding security engagement with Somalia and its prospective contribution to AUSSOM have introduced further sensitivity into discussions about troop deployments. The African Union’s June 2025 negotiations with troop-contributing countries included Ethiopia and Egypt, demonstrating that both countries were considered within the mission’s institutional arrangements. In December 2025, the African Union also acknowledged Egypt’s preparations for deployment while emphasizing the need to prevent security gaps during the transition. Political endorsement, negotiated contributions and actual troop deployments, however, remain distinct stages. For Ethiopia, any substantial expansion of Egyptian forces near areas where Ethiopian troops operate would raise operational questions, particularly given the unresolved Nile dispute. Careful coordination would be essential to prevent competing strategic interests from complicating counterterrorism operations. Kenya faces a related challenge arising from Somalia’s domestic political confrontation. Laftagareen’s presence in Kenya following his removal has generated criticism from Somali officials. On October 19, Somalia’s parliamentary speaker, Abdikadir Mohamed Nur Jama, reportedly accused individuals residing in Kenya of involvement in activities connected to the conflict and questioned the alleged protection they received. The reporting did not establish evidence supporting those allegations, and Kenyan authorities had not publicly responded at the time. Hosting Somali political figures does not independently demonstrate Kenyan government support for their military activities. Nairobi must balance its diplomatic responsibilities and continued cooperation with Mogadishu against its own legal and national security considerations. The consequences of Somali instability for Kenya are also economic. The Lamu Port South Sudan Ethiopia Transport corridor, LAPSSET, represents an important regional infrastructure initiative intended to expand commercial connectivity and diversify access to maritime trade. Its security is connected to conditions in northern and coastal Kenya, where Al Shabaab has demonstrated the ability to threaten personnel and transport infrastructure. On September 19, 2026, suspected militants attacked Kenyan military personnel patrolling part of the corridor in Garissa. No casualties were reported, but the incident illustrated the security demands associated with protecting strategic infrastructure. Although these attacks cannot be directly attributed to the South West State’s political crisis, prolonged instability in Somalia could place additional pressure on counterterrorism operations and create opportunities for militant expansion. For Kenya, preserving security cooperation with Somalia therefore carries implications for domestic security, investment and regional transport connectivity. Ethiopia shares an interest in protecting these connections, which could strengthen economic integration and provide additional commercial routes. Against this background, the partnership between Addis Ababa and Nairobi offers continuity. Cooperation in electricity transmission, telecommunications and transport has created practical interests that extend beyond individual political disagreements. During his October 20 visit , Abiy emphasized Ethiopia’s electricity exports to Kenya, Safaricom’s presence in Ethiopia and growing commercial connections. Their importance becomes greater as Ethiopia confronts renewed tensions with Eritrea, instability in northern Ethiopia and unresolved strategic disagreements with Egypt. The October 2026 escalation in Tigray and tensions with Eritrea demonstrate the competing pressures confronting Addis Ababa. Strong relations with Kenya provide an additional channel for diplomatic consultation without requiring both governments to adopt identical policies toward Somalia. The coming months will test whether the three countries can prevent Somalia’s internal confrontation from developing into a wider regional dispute. Particular attention should be given to the security situation around Baidoa, changes to Ethiopian and Egyptian troop arrangements, and Somalia’s political preparations ahead of the presidential election announced for May 15, 2027 . Diplomatic engagement through Kenya, IGAD or other regional mechanisms could become increasingly relevant if political divisions deepen. Whether mediation initiatives emerge, however, will depend on the willingness of the parties to pursue negotiation. Abiy’s Kenya visit ultimately illustrates the continuing value of dependable regional partnerships during a period of uncertainty. Ethiopia’s national interests require a stable Somalia, effective cooperation against Al Shabaab and security arrangements that do not unnecessarily entangle Ethiopian forces in domestic political rivalries. Its relationship with Kenya offers opportunities to advance those objectives while protecting economic integration and regional connectivity. The challenge for Addis Ababa is to preserve this partnership alongside constructive engagement with Mogadishu, ensuring that Somalia’s political disagreements do not become another source of confrontation across the Horn of Africa. A comparison of the IGAD facilitated process that produced the 1988 agreement with the Turkish brokered Ankara Declaration of December 2024 reveals both the continuity of Ethiopia’s core security interests and the shifting diplomatic environment in which those interests are pursued. The confrontation that shaped the 1980s negotiations originated in the aftermath of the 1977–78 Ogaden War. Somalia continued to assert territorial claims over the Ogaden region of Ethiopia. Mutual destabilization compounded by internal pressures on both regimes produced a protracted period of tension short of renewed full scale interstate war. At the inaugural IGAD summit in Djibouti in January 1986 Ethiopian leader Mengistu Haile Mariam and Somali President Siad Barre established a joint ad hoc ministerial committee to examine the sources of bilateral discord. Although the committee was formally joint Ethiopia’s representatives led at key sessions by Foreign Minister Lt-Col. Goshu Wolde consistently prioritized recognition of existing international boundaries and the cessation of support for anti Ethiopian groups. This agenda setting approach shaped the substance of the talks. Somalia preferred to sequence confidence building measures troop disengagement restoration of diplomatic relations and prisoner exchanges before addressing the boundary question. Three principal ministerial sessions took place in May 1986 August 1986 and April 1987. Progress remained limited because of these differing priorities. A further meeting between the two heads of state on the margins of the March 1988 IGAD summit in Djibouti provided the decisive political impetus. The resulting agreement formalized after talks in Mogadishu on 3 and 4 April 1988 restored diplomatic relations provided for the withdrawal of security forces from the border ended hostile propaganda terminated mutual support for insurgent groups and arranged the exchange of prisoners of war. Both sides agreed to discuss the boundary question at a later date. In practice the accord ended active Somali claims on the Ogaden and secured Ethiopia’s south eastern frontier freeing Ethiopian resources for pressing internal challenges. The 1988 agreement demonstrated that a regional structure could deliver tangible results when the parties shared a pragmatic interest in stabilizing a disputed border and when one party Ethiopia articulated its security requirements with clarity and consistency. No open interstate war between Ethiopia and Somalia occurred after 1988. Somalia’s subsequent state collapse created a different environment. Under Prime Minister Meles Zenawi Ethiopia engaged constructively in efforts to rebuild Somali institutions helping to shape the transitional federal structure that emerged in the absence of a functioning central authority. This engagement responded first to immediate security concerns arising from the political space along Ethiopia’s border. At the same time it reinforced Ethiopia’s standing as a constructive regional actor. When the Islamic Courts Union consolidated control over much of southern Somalia in 2006 and posed a direct security challenge Ethiopia intervened in support of the Transitional Federal Government. Limited deployments earlier that year preceded full scale action in December 2006. That intervention reflected continuity rather than rupture Ethiopia acted to prevent hostile forces from establishing themselves in adjacent ungoverned space. Serious bilateral tension re emerged only in 2024 following the January memorandum of understanding between Ethiopia and Somaliland concerning commercial and naval access to the sea. Somalia denounced the arrangement as a violation of its territorial integrity, recalled its ambassador and explicitly rejected African Union mediation efforts conditioning any engagement on Ethiopia’s retraction of the memorandum. This stance effectively limited the immediate scope for regional bodies including IGAD to facilitate dialogue on a dispute touching core sovereignty claims. The political climate had become more transactional with parties weighing concrete exchanges of interests rather than operating within the denser shared outlooks of earlier periods. The Ankara Declaration of 11–12 December 2024 facilitated by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, produced a de escalation. The leaders reaffirmed respect for each other’s sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity. They acknowledged the potential benefits of Ethiopia’s assured access to and from the sea while affirming that any commercial arrangements would operate under the sovereign authority of the Federal Republic of Somalia. Technical negotiations were scheduled to begin no later than the end of February 2025 and to conclude within four months with Turkish facilitation available as needed. IGAD welcomed the declaration as a constructive step toward regional stability that external facilitation can complement rather than displace regional mechanisms when circumstances require additional diplomatic weight. In the mid 1980s member state cohesion a bipolar international context that channeled regional diplomacy and a shared interest in border stability enabled IGAD to serve as an effective vehicle. Ethiopia acting within that institutional framework advanced outcomes consistent with its security requirements. Three decades later protracted state fragility in Somalia internal challenges across several Horn countries and the proliferation of external actors with diverse interests altered the diplomacy. Regional organizations continue to perform important roles however on certain sovereignty laden disputes their immediate leverage may be constrained. Ethiopia’s posture has remained consistent across these decades safeguarding the south eastern frontier preventing the establishment of hostile actors in adjacent ungoverned spaces and securing reliable access to the sea. The instruments joint committees under a regional umbrella support for transitional governance calibrated military engagement when necessary and pragmatic external facilitation have adapted to changing conditions. In 2024 Turkish mediation filled a temporary institutional vacuum created by the particular constraints facing regional mechanisms on this sovereignty sensitive question. The 1988 accord and the 2024 Ankara Declaration both illustrate that durable progress depends less on the formal identity of the mediator than on the alignment of core interests and the availability of credible channels for dialogue. It highlights the consistency of Ethiopia's core security interests while adapting to changing diplomatic contexts, illustrated by the 1988 agreement and the 2024 Ankara Declaration. The 1988 agreement, facilitated by IGAD, marked a significant step in stabilizing relations by addressing border disputes and ending mutual support for insurgent groups. In contrast, the 2024 Ankara Declaration, brokered by Turkey, aimed to de-escalate tensions following Ethiopia's agreement with Somaliland, which Somalia viewed as a threat to its sovereignty. The article emphasizes that successful mediation relies on aligning core interests and establishing credible dialogue channels, regardless of the mediator's identity. Overall, Ethiopia's approach has remained focused on safeguarding its territorial integrity and regional stability.

Convened in late 1996 under IGAD’s newly established conflict-resolution mandate, the talks culminated on 3 January 1997 in the creation of a 41-member National Salvation Council, with representation allocated to the four major clan families and smaller communities. Although Sodere did not produce a lasting government, it established a broad-based framework for political representation that subsequent reconciliation efforts would revisit The collapse of the Somali state in January 1991 left political authority dispersed among armed factions, while successive international efforts failed to establish a national government capable of consolidating control. The Addis Ababa Agreement of 1993 brought leading factions into a common framework, but agreement on paper did not resolve the struggle for power in Mogadishu; by the time the last United Nations troops withdrew in March 1995, the underlying competition remained intact. Rivalry between Ali Mahdi Mohamed and the Aideed camp, which passed to Hussein Aideed following General Mohamed Farah Aideed’s death in August 1996, continued to obstruct the emergence of a national political authority. The consequences extended beyond the capital. In the border region of Gedo, Al-Itihaad al-Islamiya (AIAI) established a presence centered on Luuq, roughly ninety kilometers from Ethiopia, which Addis Ababa regarded as a base for a movement responsible for attacks inside Ethiopia and linked to other armed groups opposed to its government. Somalia’s fragmentation thus presented Ethiopia with a problem that international mediation alone had not resolved, the absence of a functioning state was not merely prolonging conflict within Somalia but also leaving neighboring territory exposed to armed networks that could operate across the border. This gave Ethiopia a direct security interest in the restoration of Somali political authority. The expansion of regional institutions in 1996 provided an important foundation for a more coordinated response to Somalia’s political fragmentation, creating a framework through which Ethiopia could address its security concerns while contributing to a regional effort to restore Somali political dialogue. Founded in 1986 as the Intergovernmental Authority on Drought and Development, with a mandate centred on drought and desertification, the organization was reconstituted as the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD) following the amendment of its founding instrument in Nairobi on 21 March 1996 and its relaunch at the Djibouti summit of 25–26 November. The revised charter incorporated the prevention, management and resolution of inter-state and intra-state conflicts through dialogue, placing peace and security alongside food security and economic cooperation among the organization’s priorities. This change reflected a broader recognition that the conflicts confronting the Horn of Africa required regional mechanisms capable of addressing their political and security dimensions. For Ethiopia, whose border security was directly affected by the absence of effective authority in Somalia, IGAD’s expanded mandate offered a legitimate avenue for supporting reconciliation through regional diplomacy. The framework connected Ethiopia’s immediate security concerns with the wider regional interest in reducing conflict and restoring political order in Somalia, giving its diplomatic engagement an institutional foundation and a shared regional purpose. Although divisions among IGAD members, including the severance of relations with Sudan by Ethiopia, Eritrea and Uganda during the preceding year, complicated regional cooperation, the organization’s expanded mandate established an important basis for renewed engagement. OAU strengthened this framework in July 1996, when its Yaoundé resolution recognized Meles Zenawi, then outgoing OAU chairman, as holding a special mandate to facilitate peace in Somalia and supported efforts by IGAD member states to reactivate their initiatives. This endorsement connected the emerging regional effort to the OAU’s broader diplomatic role and reinforced the legitimacy of renewed attempts to bring Somali factions into negotiations. Ethiopia subsequently informed the United Nations Security Council that it had convened the Sodere conference in November 1996 in accordance with an IGAD mandate. Operating within this reinforced regional framework, Ethiopian conduct in the second half of 1996 ran along two tracks that differed in instrument yet converged through local partnerships. On the military track, Ethiopia acted against Al-Itihaad al-Islamiya (AIAI), an Islamist group that had established a presence in the Gedo region centered on Luuq, roughly ninety kilometres from the Ethiopian border. Addis Ababa regarded AIAI as a direct security threat, holding it responsible for attacks inside Ethiopia and linking it to other armed networks opposed to the Ethiopian government. Ethiopian forces therefore crossed into Gedo on 9 August 1996 to attack AIAI bases, and fighting continued through December. The fourth major assault on the group, launched on 11 June 1997, captured Luuq and Buulo Haawo and deprived AIAI of its last major bases in the region. This military campaign ran in parallel with a political initiative that sought to harness Somali opposition to AIAI and embed Ethiopia’s border-security objectives within a broader reconciliation process. On the political track, Ethiopia convened Somali leaders at the Sodere resort for roughly six weeks of talks, which ended on 3 January 1997 with a declaration signed by 27 leaders representing 26 factions. The declaration created a National Salvation Council of 41 members and a National Executive Committee of 11 members led by five co-chairmen, with authority to speak for the Council and to prepare a Transitional Central Authority or Provisional Central Government, and it committed the signatories to a National Reconciliation Conference at Bossaso. The Somali National Front, a competitor of AIAI for control of Gedo, was among the signatories. That overlap offered Somali opponents of AIAI an institutional route to national standing and tied a border security objective to a political process that Somali actors could own. The composition of the Council contains the process’s most durable contribution. Nine seats went to each of the four major clan families, Darod, Hawiye, Rahanweyn and Dir, and five to smaller groups, a distribution that totals 41 and approximates the half-share later formalized for minorities under the 4.5 formula. For the first time the Darod accepted parity among the main clan families. That principle of clan-family parity, first given institutional expression at Sodere, was subsequently formalized at the Arta conference in 2000 and then applied at scale by the Mbagathi process, which in 2004 allocated 61 seats to each of the four major families and 31 to the minority bloc within a 275-member Transitional Federal Parliament. By converting a contest over who speaks for Somalia into a bounded negotiation over who sits within each family’s allotment, parity supplied the mechanism through which Sodere moved Somali politics from open military competition toward transitional institutions. Sodere’s significance extended beyond the representational framework it helped establish to the regional diplomacy through which that framework was pursued. Ethiopia’s subsequent involvement in Somali reconciliation formed part of a recurring pattern that included hosting the 1993 Addis Ababa conference, convening Sodere in 1996 and 1997, participating in the IGAD-mediated Mbagathi talks that produced the Transitional Federal Charter in 2004, and contributing troops to the African Union missions in Somalia, AMISOM and ATMIS, and now AUSSOM. The Mbagathi record offers particularly clear evidence that Somali actors themselves regarded Ethiopia’s participation as consequential. In February 2004, six faction leaders of the Somali Restoration and Reconstruction Council announced that they would stay out of the final phase of the talks while Ethiopia was absent from the table. Hussein Aideed, who had succeeded his father General Mohamed Farah Aideed in 1996 and had remained outside the Sodere process the following year, now argued that a regional peace process required consensus among neighbouring states as well as among Somalis. His position marked a shift from contesting Ethiopia’s involvement in 1997 to treating the participation of neighboring states as a condition of a credible settlement, illustrating how the regional approach embodied at Sodere became an established feature of subsequent Somali peace negotiations. This historical experience has direct relevance as Somalia confronts a demanding security transition, with Al-Shabaab continuing to threaten state consolidation, domestic political negotiations remaining unsettled after the inconclusive May 2026 talks, and AUSSOM’s operational future facing growing financial uncertainty following Washington’s announced intention to end its support for UN logistics and operations from 2027. Ethiopia’s renewed commitment to AUSSOM, reaffirmed at the August 2026 troop-contributing countries summit, provides an important basis for strengthening this regional security relationship. Somalia’s current security transition increases the strategic importance of sustained coordination with Ethiopia. Al-Shabaab retains a presence in areas of Gedo and Bakool near the Ethiopian frontier, while Washington’s decision to end funding for UN logistical support to AUSSOM after December 2026 adds pressure to the mission’s operational continuity. These developments connect Somalia’s internal security challenges directly to the management of its western border, where gaps in territorial control can enable armed groups to move, reorganize and exploit weaknesses in coordination between security forces. Ethiopia’s direct exposure to these threats, its existing security involvement in Somalia and its capacity to operate along the shared frontier make bilateral cooperation consequential to how these risks are managed. For Mogadishu, the practical priority is to establish predictable arrangements with Addis Ababa for intelligence exchange, border threat assessment, troop coordination and consultation over operations affecting Somali territory. These mechanisms would help align Ethiopian security activities with federal priorities, improve continuity between bilateral cooperation and AUSSOM, and give Somali authorities greater influence over the regional response to threats within their jurisdiction. As Somalia assumes greater responsibility for its own security amid uncertainty over international support, the quality of its coordination with Ethiopia will directly affect its capacity to manage cross-border threats and sustain security across its western regions. ethiopia.summary: The Ethiopia-Djibouti Trade Corridor is crucial for both nations, with over 95% of Ethiopia's trade relying on this route, which also significantly supports Djibouti's economy. Recent tensions, particularly the TPLF-Shabiya's attempts to disrupt this corridor, pose risks not only to Ethiopia's economic stability but also to Djibouti's port revenues. The Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) has shown military superiority, yet threats to the corridor highlight vulnerabilities that could be exploited by opposing forces. The situation underscores the need for enhanced bilateral security cooperation and integrated defense strategies to protect this vital infrastructure. Recent military developments, including the ENDF's counteroffensive, have temporarily reversed rebel advances, but ongoing vigilance and coordinated efforts are essential to ensure the corridor's security and maintain regional stability.

ethiopia.content: Except War, What Option is Ethiopia Left With to Defend Persistent Incursions from Eritrea? – HORN REVIEW Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us Search Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us 2026-10-21 Except War, What Option is Ethiopia Left With to Defend Persistent Incursions from Eritrea? 0 Comments Having learned from the devastating costs of the 1998 border war between Ethiopia and Eritrea and the 2020 northern Ethiopia conflict, preventing a full-scale war between Ethiopia and Eritrea remains crucial. In a region plagued by persistent conflict, militant activities, and extremist and terrorist havens, the last thing it needs is another war. As U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated , “the last thing the world needs right now is another war.” However, Ethiopia’s relationship with Eritrea does not seem likely to be resolved through conventional diplomatic assurances alone. Since its secession, Eritrea has adopted an antagonistic posture toward its largest neighbor and pursued policies that challenge Ethiopia’s security and regional interests. It has a documented record of supporting anti-Ethiopian government armed groups, providing them with sanctuary and other forms of assistance. Following the Pretoria peace agreement, although Eritrean forces withdrew from Tigray’s heartland, they remained in territories inside Tigray near the Eritrean border. Eritrea also established an alliance with the TPLF and other armed groups inside Ethiopian territory, with the latter forming an alliance aimed at overthrowing the Ethiopian federal government. In this context, Eritrea plays a significant role, while other external actors also contribute by providing support. The nature of the Eritrean state under the People’s Front for Democracy and Justice (PFDJ) remains a persistent source of insecurity for Ethiopia. The country’s political system is highly centralized and militarized, with indefinite national service, the dominance of military institutions over civilian administration, and the concentration of power in President Isaias Afwerki and his close circle all playing a central role in keeping the regime in power. Since the 1998–2000 border war, Eritrea has maintained a security posture shaped by permanent mobilization and a deep suspicion of Ethiopia. This reflects what can be described as a small-state syndrome, in which the perceived vulnerability of a state, its limited strategic depth, and its exposure to stronger neighbors shape how its leadership understands external threats. In Eritrea’s case, this outlook has reinforced the tendency to view Ethiopia through a security lens and to treat the preservation of regime security as a national priority. This reinforces the need to address the underlying strategic calculations that shape Eritrea’s behavior toward Ethiopia. In recent years, the practical consequences of this structure have become evident in Eritrea’s military presence in border areas of northern Ethiopia and its cultivation of relationships with armed groups operating inside Ethiopian territory. For more than a year, Ethiopian authorities documented patterns of material support, including ammunition intercepts and alleged training linkages, directed toward elements of the Tigray People’s Liberation Front and other armed groups in Ethiopia. These activities culminated in formal Ethiopian notifications to the United Nations Security Council in October 2026, invoking Article 51 of the UN Charter on the inherent right of self-defense in response to the advances of Eritrean units tens of kilometers into Tigrayan territory and coordination with domestic insurgent coalitions. The severing of diplomatic relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara in early October further removed remaining formal channels for crisis management. In this environment, Eritrea’s conduct has shifted from wartime alliance against the TPLF during 2020–2022 to a tactical realignment that treats a weakened or fragmented Ethiopian center as preferable to a consolidated neighbor capable of projecting power in the region. The nature of the regime, shaped by President Isaias Afwerki’s personalized style of rule and his longstanding political outlook towards Ethiopia, makes it unlikely that Asmara will voluntarily provide the guarantees necessary for de-escalation. For Ethiopia, however, Isaias’s decades-long rule has remained a persistent security concern, given Eritrea’s history of hostility towards its southern neighbor and its support for armed with anti-government agendas. Ethiopia needs credible guarantees from Eritrea to address these concerns, ease tensions, and create conditions for a lasting resolution. However, as noted above, the nature of Eritrea’s leadership makes such guarantees difficult to secure, particularly if they require a change in the security policies and political outlook that have shaped its approach towards Ethiopia for decades. Demands for an end to support for armed opposition groups, the cessation of cross-border arms transfers, and a verifiable halt to military preparations near Ethiopian territory would require the Eritrean leadership to reconsider practices closely tied to its system of internal control. Introduced during the 1998–2000 border war, national service has evolved into an indefinite obligation serving both military and labor needs. Many Eritreans remain in service for years, often with little control over their assignments and limited remuneration. Its prolonged nature also gives the government considerable influence over citizens’ livelihoods and their ability to leave state service. In Eritrea, generals often wield greater authority than civilian officials at the zonal level, with power ultimately concentrated in the presidency. Isaias Afwerki has also rotated military commanders and senior officials, limiting their ability to build independent power bases. Control over the economy, political coordination, information, and national security remains concentrated among a small circle of trusted figures whose influence depends heavily on their relationship with the president. Under such conditions, transparency and demobilization would be perceived as a threat to the regime’s capacity to extract resources, suppress dissent, and justify isolation. The empirical record of Eritrean foreign policy since its secession, marked by disputes with Yemen, Djibouti, Sudan, and Ethiopia, illustrates a consistent preference for confrontation over institutionalized cooperation when the latter would constrain personalist authority. In essence, full-scale war between Ethiopia and Eritrea would risk repeating the cost of the previous conflicts, while increasing the risk of regional actors becoming involved. A direct war between Ethiopia and Eritrea would be an uneven contest given Ethiopia’s demographic and military scale. Yet Eritrea’s garrison-state structure would allow it to mobilize much of its population and national resources with potentially devastating consequences for its population and economy. Therefore, Ethiopia’s dilemma would be how to neutralize the threat posed by Eritrea’s leadership without turning the military imbalance into a prolonged and costly conflict. Given these constraints, effective threat neutralization begins with identifying the specific sources of risk. These include Eritrea’s military presence, support for armed groups, and other activities directed by its leadership that threaten Ethiopia’s security. Given the concentration of political and security authority within Eritrea’s leadership, a surgical and swift operation directed at the narrow decision-making and security core offers a theoretically coherent pathway. The personalist character of the Eritrean system concentrates operational and political authority in a limited set of individuals and institutions surrounding the president. However, this approach would require a carefully defined communication strategy to establish the basis for action, build international understanding of its security concerns and demonstrate that any measures taken are necessary and proportionate to the threats identified. Israel’s approach towards Iran illustrates how operations targeting senior leadership and key decision-making structures can disrupt command arrangements and weaken a state’s capacity to coordinate its response. However, Iran’s institutional depth has allowed it to sustain resistance despite the loss of senior figures. Eritrea differs in this respect, but the case provides an illustration. Its political system is more personalized, with authority concentrated around Isaias Afwerki and a narrow circle of military and security officials. Let alone the removal of the inner circle, the removal of Isaias would be consequential extending beyond Ethiopia’s immediate security concerns, potentially reshaping Eritrea’s political order and the wider Horn of Africa. Eritrea’s relatively shallow administrative depth, compared with more layered systems that possess provincial redundancy or institutionalized revolutionary guards, may increase the disruptive potential of precise action against the center. For international actors, Eritrea’s status as a pariah state, its record of playing a spoiler role in the region, and its government’s persistent human rights violations would shape how they assess such a development. The prospect of a change in leadership could be viewed as an opportunity to address longstanding sources of regional instability and the country’s human rights crisis. In its 2015 report, the UN Commission of Inquiry on Human Rights in Eritrea found that “systematic, widespread and gross human rights violations have been and are being committed in Eritrea under the authority of the Government,” adding that some of these violations “may constitute crimes against humanity.” Beyond this, such an approach could help avert a devastating interstate war, free the Eritrean people from a tyrannical and deeply oppressive regime and minimize wider humanitarian consequences. The broader regional context reinforces the logic of limitation. A major war would intersect with ongoing conflicts in Sudan, competition over Red Sea access, and Nile water disputes, creating opportunities for external actors to deeply embed themselves in the region. Eritrea’s alignment with SAF’s al-Burhan and Egypt mean that uncontrolled escalation would quickly expand the geographic and political scope of the conflict. By contrast, a tightly constrained operation that demonstrably prioritizes the neutralization of leadership-directed threats minimizes the grounds for third-party intervention and preserves Ethiopia’s capacity to address internal security challenges. The small-state syndrome that shapes Eritrean behavior is characterized by acute sensitivity to Ethiopia’s growing regional role and influence, alongside a tendency to use asymmetric means to constrain Ethiopia’s position and establish strategic buffer zones along its borders including through support for the TPLF. As noted, Eritrea’s political and security system is built around military mobilization, secrecy, and the use of regional networks to advance its strategic interests. For Ethiopia to achieve lasting security, Eritrea would need to provide credible assurances against military build-up, arms trafficking, and support for proxy groups, including the TPLF and other armed movements, while preventing its territory from being used as a sanctuary for groups seeking to destabilize Ethiopia. However, the centralized and highly personalized nature of Isaias Afwerki’s rule raises serious doubts about whether such commitments would be honored without meaningful pressure. Ethiopia’s long-term security interests therefore depend on addressing these sources of interference while avoiding the heavy costs of a prolonged interstate war. A carefully considered approach, supported by verified intelligence and a coherent communication strategy, seeks to address immediate security threats while preserving the prospects for long-term regional stability. Ethiopia cannot afford to remain trapped in the same recurring cycle of confrontation with Eritrea, in which unresolved threats repeatedly generate new tensions and bring both countries closer to a devastating war. Eritrea's support for anti-Ethiopian armed groups and its military presence near the border exacerbate tensions. Opening the three-day capacity development workshop today, Ethiopia's Auditor General Meseret Damtie said strengthening African Supreme Audit Institutions (SAIs) is essential in order to promote accountable governance, sound public financial management and sustainable development across the continent. She emphasized that improved audit quality, institutional capacity and collaboration are essential to enable audit institutions fulfil their mandates effectively. "At the heart of ARISE (African Regional Initiative for Strengthening Effectiveness) is the spirit of peer support and collaboration," the Auditor General said, highlighting the importance of cooperation among participating institutions, programme coordinators, peer SAIs and development partners in achieving sustainable results. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn She said the workshop provides an opportunity to clarify roles and responsibilities, strengthen project-management and facilitation skills, and exchange experiences from the programme's early implementation. Meseret linked the principles of cooperation and collective responsibility underpinning ARISE to Ethiopia's Medemer philosophy, which emphasizes synergy, shared contributions and common goals. She highlighted the importance of collaboration in strengthening institutions and advancing sustainable development, reflecting the program's emphasis on partnerships and collective efforts to improve public-sector accountability across Africa. INTOSAI Development Initiative (IDI) representative, Muhammed Dabo, stressed that sustainable improvements in Supreme Audit Institutions require more than technical training, emphasizing strong institutional systems, effective leadership, capable personnel and the ability to manage change. "Each partner has a distinct role, but we share one objective: stronger, more effective and sustainable Supreme Audit Institutions," he said, underscoring the complementary roles of beneficiary SAIs, peer institutions, regional organizations and development partners. Dabo encouraged the participants to share experiences openly, identify challenges early, adapt when necessary and develop practical solutions for their respective institutions. He stressed that the workshop's success should be measured by the lessons applied and improvements achieved after participants return to their work. During an interview with the Ethiopian Broadcasting Corporation (EBC), he said the TPLF violated the Pretoria Agreement signed in October 2022. The PM recalled that the key elements of the Pretoria Agreement included cessation of hostilities, restoration of all services, disarmament, return of displaced people, and recognition of the constitutional order. On the contrary, the TPLF had been purchasing and soliciting weapons as well as openly recruiting young people instead of implementing the agreement to disarm combatants. Above all, PM Abiy pointed out that after the agreement, the TPLF used displaced persons as hostages to prevent them from returning to their homes. Additionally, it engaged in destroying and closing down infrastructure--including airlines, banking, and telecommunications--that had been restored by the Federal Government to deliver services. Despite the group's misdeeds, the PM stated that the government had forewarned that war was not worthwhile and that peace was preferable. However, the TPLF disregarded the advice and collaborated with various forces, and violated the Pretoria Agreement by initiating an unnecessary war. Immense damage has been inflicted on the public as a result of the war instigated by the TPLF, he noted. War is bad and yields no benefit, the Premier further noted, adding that a war fought for the interests of foreign forces is even worse. The psychological damage is not to be taken lightly and damage has also been inflicted on development and the economy. Taye underscored the importance of reliable statistics in driving evidence-based development in Africa. Addressing the opening of the 10th Session of the Statistical Commission for Africa and the 12th Meeting of the Regional Committee of the United Nations Global Geospatial Information Management for Africa in Addis Ababa, the President said Ethiopia's development planning is anchored in measurable targets and reliable data. He emphasized that development cannot be effectively planned, sustained, or scaled up without accurate measurement, noting that official statistics are essential for shaping development strategies, tracking progress, and strengthening accountability. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines The President also highlighted Ethiopia's reforms in the financial and digital sectors, including the National Digital Payment Strategy, financial sector liberalization, interoperable payment infrastructure, and the national digital identification program, Fayda. He said Fayda enables secure electronic verification and expands access to banking, mobile money, telecommunications, and other essential public services, demonstrating how digital infrastructure can improve service delivery and financial inclusion. According to the President, mobile money and mobile banking accounts in Ethiopia reached 257 million and processed more than 24 trillion birr in transactions during the first nine months of 2026, reflecting the expansion of the country's financial and digital systems. Drawing lessons from these reforms, he stressed that statistics must serve as practical tools for sustainable development and be communicated clearly and accessibly to policymakers and citizens, rather than being treated as an end in themselves. He also called for statistical institutions to integrate and safeguard diverse data sources without compromising statistical integrity, emphasizing that innovation must reinforce data quality, institutional independence, and public trust. The President urged African governments to protect the professional independence of official statistics, strengthen legal and institutional frameworks, invest in national statistical systems, and ground policy decisions in scientific evidence. He cautioned that poor-quality data undermines evidence-based policymaking, impedes development, and weakens accountability. somalia.content: Somalia aviation authority, IATA sign agreement to strengthen safety oversight - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS Somalia aviation authority, IATA sign agreement to strengthen safety oversight Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Monday October 19, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) — Somalia’s civil aviation authority and the International Air Transport Association (IATA) signed an agreement to strengthen aviation safety oversight, including recognition of two internationally used audit programs for airlines and ground operations. The memorandum of understanding (MoU) was signed Saturday in Mogadishu by Transport and Civil Aviation Minister Mohamed Farah Nuh, Somali Civil Aviation Authority Director General Ahmed Moallim Hassan and Kamil Alawadhi, IATA’s regional vice president for Africa and the Middle East. advertisements Under the agreement, the Somali Civil Aviation Authority will recognize the IATA Operational Safety Audit (IOSA) and the IATA Safety Audit for Ground Operations (ISAGO) as acceptable means of compliance with national regulations, complementing its own safety oversight functions. The programs will complement, rather than replace, the authority’s own regulatory and safety oversight functions. “Global safety standards are the cornerstone of efficient and safe operations. Through this MoU, we will work with the Somali CAA towards the continuous improvement of safety standards, promote the adoption of industry best practices, and foster a culture of safety across the aviation sector. This partnership reflects our mutual dedication to advancing aviation safety for the benefit of passengers, operators and the wider aviation industry in Somalia and Africa,” said Kamil Alawadhi, IATA’s Regional Vice President for Africa and Middle East. IOSA is an internationally recognized audit system designed to assess an airline’s operational management and control systems. More than 450 airlines are currently listed on the IOSA registry, and all IATA member airlines are required to maintain IOSA registration. ISAGO applies similar standardized oversight to companies providing ground-handling services at airports. IATA says the program is intended to reduce operational risks, improve consistency in ground handling and limit duplication between audits conducted by airlines, airports and regulators. The agreement forms part of IATA’s Focus Africa initiative, which includes efforts to improve aviation safety, infrastructure, connectivity and regulatory standards across the continent. The agreement signed in Mogadishu comes as authorities continue rebuilding a civil aviation system that was severely weakened after the collapse of the central government in 1991. The country has gradually reestablished national control over aviation functions, including management of Somali airspace and regulatory oversight of airlines and airports. somalia.content: Families fleeing Somalia crises find bleak prospects in Dadaab refugee camps - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS Families fleeing Somalia crises find bleak prospects in Dadaab refugee camps Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Tuesday October 20, 2026 Nurto fled conflict in Baidoa and is struggling to support her seven children in Dadaab refugee camps/Ahmed Abdulahi/Ergo Families fleeing adversity in different parts of southern Somalia have been arriving in Kenya’s Dadaab refugee camps, where they find themselves with no means of making a living nor aid or support. They include families fleeing conflict in Baidoa, house demolitions by the Somali government in Mogadishu, and drought in their home areas. advertisements The new arrivals say they have received no reception support, shelter, or other forms of aid. Some are staying with relatives already struggling to make ends meet, while others have settled on their own on vacant land in Dadaab’s Ifo-2 camp. They lack food, housing, toilets and other basic services. Nurto Mohamed Ali, who arrived in Ifo-2 on 20 August, said her family had received no assistance and was struggling to meet basic needs. She is staying with relatives who arrived earlier. “Neighbours collect maize and cooking oil for us. That is how we are surviving now,” she said. “We have children who need food and bedding, but we have nothing to give them.” Nurto fled ongoing conflict in Baidoa between federal government forces and those loyal to the former South West State administration. She was a farmer raising her family on their two-hectare plot of land in Baidoa. Separated from her husband, she receives no support from him and is the sole income earner. In the refugee camp now, her seven children often go to bed hungry because she lacks food. They occupy a shelter made from plastic sheets, cloth and thorny branches in the yard of a relatives’ home – a household of 10. The days reach a scorching 37°C and the rainy season has begun. Nurto and her older children have to sleep outside without bedding while the youngest children cram themselves into the hut. Nurto said they had expected to receive assistance on arrival, including refugee registration cards, household items, and a house. She has received nothing. “We have no proper house, and even the people who arrived before us do not have one. The shelter situation is very difficult. We sleep on pieces of cloth and a small, broken mat,” she said. Other vulnerable new arrivals, including older people, people with disabilities, women and children, are finding no formal help in the camp, where some walk around daily asking more established residents for food. Hawo Mohamed Ali, her disabled husband, and their 10 children arrived in Ifo-2 on 1 August. They fled Mogadishu’s Hodan district after the government demolished their house, saying the land belonged to the state. They had lived in the house for 34 years without having formal land ownership documents. She said losing the home made it impossible for her family to remain in Mogadishu. “When we left and went outside, we found our land fenced off and surrounded by a wall,” she told Radio Ergo. “We were told the land would be measured and returned to us. Our houses were demolished using bulldozers, and we thought the land would be given back. Later, we were told it was government land and that we had to leave.” The demolition left Hawo’s family homeless and they decided their only option was to seek refuge in Dadaab. In Mogadishu, she earned a living selling meat and watermelon in local markets. In the refugee camp, however, they have not been registered and haven’t received aid cards or assistance. She looked for laundry work, but the jobs are irregular, so she has to ask others for help with food for her children. She lacks firewood and containers for collecting water. “The children’s father is disabled, and life is very difficult for us. My children are still young and have nothing here. We left our home and came to a place we do not know,” said Hawo, adding that the conditions in Dadaab were far worse than she had expected. The chairman of Hagardera camp, Khalif Dhubow Jelle, said the hardship facing new arrivals from Somalia had been brought to the attention of humanitarian agencies in the camps, but no effective response had followed. He recorded nearly 250 families having arrived from southern Somalia in the past three months. “Their living conditions are extremely poor. It is also the rainy season, yet these people have no shelter or place to stay. They are sitting in the open and have no food or water,” he said. The new arrivals are joining a refugee population already struggling with difficult living conditions because of reduced humanitarian aid and wider economic hardship across the camps. somalia.summary: Families fleeing crises in Somalia are facing dire conditions in the Dadaab refugee camps in Kenya. The camps, originally established to accommodate a temporary influx of refugees, are now home to over 200,000 people, leading to overcrowding and limited resources. Many refugees are struggling with inadequate access to food, clean water, and healthcare. The ongoing conflict, drought, and famine in Somalia have driven families to seek safety, but the camps offer little hope for a better future. Aid organizations are overwhelmed and unable to meet the growing needs of the population, leaving many refugees in a state of uncertainty and despair. The situation highlights the urgent need for international support and sustainable solutions to address the challenges faced by displaced families.
